presentation: Vaccinated woman invited for cervical screening
stem:
A 25-year-old woman received the HPV vaccine at school when she was 12. She has now received her first invitation for cervical screening and tells her GP she plans to ignore it, because she has been vaccinated and has had only one sexual partner.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Screening is not needed, as the vaccine prevents every case of cervical cancer in vaccinated women
options.B: She can skip screening for as long as she stays with a single partner
options.C: Screening is only needed if she develops bleeding or unusual discharge
options.D: She should attend, as the vaccine does not cover every high-risk type
options.E: She should delay screening until she has had a booster dose of vaccine

correct_answer: D. She should attend, as the vaccine does not cover every high-risk type
why_correct: The HPV vaccine greatly reduces the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not protect against every high-risk HPV type and cannot treat infection already present. Vaccinated women are therefore still invited for cervical screening, which is the way to detect cell changes early. NHS advice is that it remains important to attend screening after vaccination. Source: NHS.uk, HPV vaccine (page last reviewed 1 September 2023).
why_wrong: A. The vaccine reduces cancer risk very substantially but does not prevent every case, so this overstates its protection and would lead to missed screening. B. Risk of HPV exposure is not removed by having one partner, since the partner may carry the virus, and screening eligibility depends on age rather than relationship status. C. Screening is meant for women without symptoms; waiting for bleeding or discharge defeats its purpose of finding changes early. E. There is no booster dose of HPV vaccine to wait for, and screening is not delayed by vaccination status.
pearl: Vaccination lowers the risk of cervical cancer; it does not replace cervical screening.
thinking: Vaccinated at school, now invited for screening  ↓  Vaccine covers the main high-risk HPV types, not all  ↓  Protection is not complete  ↓  Still attend screening
exam_trap: Assuming a vaccinated woman is fully protected and can decline screening.
takeaway: Women vaccinated against HPV should still attend cervical screening when invited.
notes: Re-angled from the bare recall 'main purpose of HPV vaccination' (near-tautological; overlaps live PAQ1149/BX items on the programme) to the practical decision that vaccination does not replace screening; same underlying learning point (vaccine prevents HPV-related cancer but is not complete protection). No live item tests this angle (searched plab1-questions.js).

presentation: Irregular tightenings in late third trimester
stem:
A 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy, a few weeks before term, telephones the maternity unit because her abdomen keeps tightening in the afternoons. The tightenings come and go, vary in strength, ease when she drinks water and rests, and have not become longer, stronger or closer together. She has had no bleeding or leaking of fluid and the baby is moving normally. In maternity triage her observations are normal, her uterus is soft between tightenings, the cervix is long and closed and the CTG is reassuring.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Threatened preterm labour needing admission for tocolysis
options.B: Concealed placental abruption with no visible vaginal bleeding
options.C: Early pre-eclampsia presenting with uterine irritability
options.E: An acute urinary tract infection triggering uterine activity

why_correct: Irregular tightenings that do not become more frequent, longer or stronger and are not accompanied by cervical change are typical of Braxton Hicks (practice) contractions. The normal observations, soft uterus between contractions, closed cervix and reassuring CTG argue against labour, abruption or other pathology. She can be reassured and told when to seek help again, for example regular painful contractions, bleeding, fluid loss or reduced movements. Source: NHS.uk, Signs that labour has begun; NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. True preterm labour needs regular painful contractions that progress with cervical change, and this woman has neither. B. Abruption causes constant pain with a hard, tender uterus and often fetal compromise, whereas her uterus is soft with a normal CTG. C. Pre-eclampsia is suggested by raised blood pressure, proteinuria or severe headache and visual symptoms, and her observations are normal. E. A urinary tract infection may cause some uterine irritability but would be suggested by urinary symptoms or fever, which she does not have.
pearl: Contractions that stay irregular and do not build, with a closed cervix, are Braxton Hicks rather than labour.
thinking: Irregular, non-progressive tightenings  ↓  Normal observations, soft uterus, closed cervix, reassuring CTG  ↓  No bleeding or fluid loss, normal movements  ↓  Braxton Hicks contractions
exam_trap: Admitting every woman with tightenings as threatened preterm labour, or missing real labour by reassuring those whose contractions are building.
takeaway: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular and do not progress, with no cervical change.
notes: Original was a short recall vignette; rebuilt with normal triage findings so the key is a diagnosis made from absence of progression, not a number. Gestation left as 'a few weeks before term' (no week threshold). Live PAQ16144 tests term latent vs established labour; Braxton Hicks only appears there as a distractor, so not a repeat.

presentation: Pill user with right upper abdominal pain and jaundice
stem:
A 29-year-old woman who has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for six years has had two days of severe pain in the right upper abdomen. Her partner noticed yesterday that her eyes look yellow, and her urine has become dark. She takes no other medicines, drinks little alcohol and has not travelled. Her temperature is 37.4°C and her blood pressure is normal.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and abdominal imaging
options.B: Reassure her that these are recognised minor effects of the pill and arrange a routine review next month
options.C: Change to a different brand of combined pill and ask her to report back if the symptoms continue
options.D: Advise simple analgesia and rest, with the symptoms to be reviewed at her next scheduled pill check
options.E: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection and review in a week

correct_answer: A. Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and abdominal imaging
why_correct: Jaundice with severe upper abdominal pain suggests a significant liver or biliary problem and needs prompt assessment with liver function tests and imaging; it should not be put down to the pill. Combined hormonal contraceptives are linked with conditions such as gallbladder disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome and liver tumours, which make them contraindicated or cautioned, so the pill should be reviewed once the cause is clear. NHS advice is that jaundice needs urgent medical assessment. Source: BNF, Ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel (contra-indications and cautions); NHS.uk, Jaundice.
why_wrong: B. Jaundice and severe pain are not minor pill effects; this reassurance would delay diagnosis of serious liver or biliary disease. C. A change of brand does nothing to investigate the cause and exposes her to the same hormones while the diagnosis is unknown. D. Analgesia and a delayed review ignores the red flag of jaundice, which needs investigation now. E. Nothing in the history points to a urinary infection, and antibiotics would not address the likely liver or biliary cause.
pearl: Jaundice in a pill user is a red flag to investigate, not a side effect to accept.
thinking: Pill user with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain  ↓  Dark urine suggests cholestasis or liver disease  ↓  Do not attribute to contraception  ↓  Same-day assessment with liver tests and imaging, then review the pill
exam_trap: Attributing jaundice and severe abdominal pain to the contraceptive pill and reassuring.
takeaway: Jaundice with abdominal pain in a woman on the pill needs same-day assessment, not reassurance.
notes: Source stem was a vague 'what should be considered' item with off-topic distractors; re-angled to a concrete next-step decision. Key is the principle (investigate promptly), not a figure. Not a live duplicate (searched plab1-questions.js for pill + jaundice). Pill-specific wording reflects BNF contra-indications/cautions; CKS page for CHC opened (Last revised in August 2024) but not quoted.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman and her partner have not conceived after 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her periods are unpredictable, coming sometimes after six weeks and sometimes after three months. She is otherwise well with a normal BMI and no pelvic pain, and her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Which blood test is most appropriate to assess the likely cause of her difficulty conceiving?

options.A: Serum FSH and luteinising hormone levels
options.B: Serum CA125 to screen for endometriosis
options.C: Chlamydia antibody testing to assess tubal damage
options.D: Thyroid peroxidase antibody level to look for autoimmunity
options.E: Serum rubella IgG to confirm her immunity status

correct_answer: A. Serum FSH and luteinising hormone levels
why_correct: Irregular cycles point towards an ovulatory disorder, so NICE advises measuring serum gonadotrophins (FSH and LH) in women with irregular cycles who are being investigated for infertility. Further tests such as prolactin are then guided by the clinical picture and results. Source: NICE NG257, Fertility problems: assessment and treatment, 2026.
why_wrong: B. CA125 is not used to diagnose endometriosis, and she has no pelvic pain to suggest it. C. Chlamydia antibodies can help to assess tubal damage, but this does not explain unpredictable cycles. D. Thyroid antibodies are not routine; thyroid function is checked only if she has symptoms of thyroid disease. E. Rubella immunity is a pre-conception check and does not explain a delay in conceiving.
pearl: In a woman with subfertility and irregular cycles, think ovulatory disorder first and check FSH and LH; prolactin is added if an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or pituitary disease is suspected.
thinking: Subfertility with unpredictable cycles  ↓  Semen analysis is normal  ↓  Suspect an ovulatory disorder  ↓  Measure serum FSH and LH
exam_trap: C, chlamydia antibody testing, is a tubal test that tempts as part of a standard subfertility work-up, but her cycle pattern points to ovulation, not tubal damage.
takeaway: Irregular cycles with subfertility call for FSH and LH to assess ovulatory function.
notes: Reframed from the AKT bare-recall item (which keyed 'ovulation' against absurd distractors) into a specific investigation decision. Key matches NG257 rec 1.18.10 (irregular cycles: serum FSH and LH). NG257 (31 March 2026) replaced CG156. No figures keyed. Near-live items differ (DT086/DR105 treatment questions; PAN2375 tubal; PAN3641 prolactinoma).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg156 (notice that CG156 is replaced by NG257)

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has had no flare for more than a year on hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolate mofetil. She and her partner would like to start a family and she asks her GP how to go about it.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop all lupus medicines now, including hydroxychloroquine, so the baby is never exposed
options.B: Try to conceive straight away and review her medicines once the pregnancy is confirmed
options.C: Arrange a planned pre-pregnancy review so unsafe medicines can be switched safely
options.D: Continue every current medicine unchanged because disease control matters most
options.E: Advise that pregnancy is unsafe in lupus and she should not try to conceive

correct_answer: C. Arrange a planned pre-pregnancy review so unsafe medicines can be switched safely
why_correct: Pregnancy is best planned when lupus is quiet, and some medicines, including mycophenolate, are harmful in pregnancy and must be changed before conception, whereas hydroxychloroquine is usually continued. A planned review with the rheumatology team allows medicines to be adjusted and specialist antenatal care to be arranged. Source: NHS.uk, Lupus (advice to see a doctor before trying to get pregnant so medicines can be checked); British Society for Rheumatology prescribing-in-pregnancy guidance (taught standard, full text not opened).
why_wrong: A. Stopping hydroxychloroquine risks a flare, which is itself harmful to mother and baby. B. Medicines must be changed before conception because mycophenolate can harm the fetus in early pregnancy. D. Some medicines, such as mycophenolate, are teratogenic and cannot simply be continued. E. Most women with well-controlled lupus can have a successful pregnancy, so pregnancy is not absolutely contraindicated.
pearl: In SLE, plan pregnancy for a time of quiet disease, switch teratogenic drugs such as mycophenolate beforehand, usually continue hydroxychloroquine and arrange specialist-led care.
thinking: SLE and planning pregnancy  ↓  Disease quiet but on mycophenolate  ↓  Teratogenic drug needs changing, hydroxychloroquine usually continued  ↓  Planned pre-pregnancy rheumatology review
exam_trap: A, stopping everything, sounds cautious but removes hydroxychloroquine, which protects against flares and is usually continued.
takeaway: Plan pregnancy in SLE with a pre-pregnancy medicines review rather than stopping all treatment or waiting for a positive test.
notes: AKT source distractor 'stop hydroxychloroquine' was the wrong direction and key was generic; reframed with a named teratogen (mycophenolate) to make the decision real. No national guideline page for SLE pregnancy could be fetched (CKS lupus 404; BSR page was a listing only; Lupus UK 404): only NHS.uk Lupus opened, so the BSR statement is standard teaching and is flagged as not opened in why_correct. Reviewer may wish to confirm against BSR 2016/2017 prescribing-in-pregnancy guideline. No live duplicate (DT158 contraception, PAQ16479 APS pregnancy).

presentation: Lower abdominal pain, woman of reproductive age
stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends the emergency department with 10 hours of lower abdominal pain, mild nausea and tenderness in the right iliac fossa. She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable, her periods are regular and her last period ended a week ago, and she uses condoms most of the time.

Which investigation should be done as part of the initial assessment before any imaging is requested?

options.A: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis

why_correct: Pregnancy status changes the differential diagnosis, since ectopic pregnancy can resemble gastrointestinal or urinary causes of pain, and it influences imaging, prescribing and surgical decisions. NICE advises being aware that women of reproductive age may be pregnant and offering a pregnancy test even when symptoms are non-specific. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. CT uses ionising radiation, so pregnancy must be excluded first and it is not the first step. B. CA125 is not a test for acute abdominal pain and is not used as an initial investigation. C. Urinalysis is useful but would not exclude pregnancy, which is the key safety check. E. A plain radiograph exposes the pelvis to radiation and rarely helps in this setting.
pearl: Think of pregnancy in every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, even when the history seems to make it unlikely; the result changes the differential, imaging and drug choices.
thinking: Woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain  ↓  Pregnancy cannot be excluded by history alone  ↓  Test before imaging or surgery  ↓  Urine pregnancy test
exam_trap: A, CT scan, is attractive when appendicitis is suspected, but it should not be done before pregnancy is excluded.
takeaway: Do a pregnancy test in all women of reproductive age with abdominal pain, whatever the history.
notes: Rewritten from the AKT why-is-pregnancy-testing-important item to a concrete action; stem deliberately gives regular periods and condom use so the stem does not cue the answer. Key follows NG126 rec 1.4.5. Live OG043/PAQ16583/PAQ1238 test known ectopic; no live item covers routine testing before imaging.

stem:
A 25-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends maternity triage at 31 weeks with three hours of painful tightenings every few minutes that are becoming stronger. Her membranes are intact and there is no vaginal bleeding. Her cervix is dilated on examination and has dilated further when the midwife re-examines her an hour later.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Braxton Hicks contractions without cervical change
options.C: Preterm prelabour rupture of the membranes
options.E: Established preterm labour needing urgent care

correct_answer: E. Established preterm labour needing urgent care
why_correct: Regular, increasingly strong contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term indicate established preterm labour. NICE defines this by progressive dilatation with regular contractions, and it triggers transfer, antenatal corticosteroids and neuroprotection decisions. Source: NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular and cause no progressive cervical change. B. Abruption usually causes constant pain, a hard uterus or bleeding, which are absent here. C. The membranes are stated to be intact, so rupture has not occurred. D. Pyelonephritis would cause fever and loin pain, and would not produce progressive cervical dilatation.
pearl: Regular contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term mean established preterm labour; the next steps are steroids, transfer to a unit with neonatal cover and magnesium sulfate at earlier gestations.
thinking: Painful contractions before term  ↓  Cervix dilating on repeat examination  ↓  Not Braxton Hicks, abruption or ruptured membranes  ↓  Established preterm labour needing urgent care
exam_trap: A, Braxton Hicks contractions, is tempting for painful tightenings in pregnancy, but they do not change the cervix.
takeaway: Contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term are established preterm labour.
notes: Re-angled from a recall definition (key restated the stem) into a differential-diagnosis vignette; the cervical-dilatation figure and the 37-week threshold are not keyed. Live PAOG027/OG055/DS135 test management of preterm labour, not the diagnosis. NG25 page lists the definition of established preterm labour (progressive dilatation from 4 cm with regular contractions), deliberately not quoted as a figure.

presentation: Severe period pain in an adolescent
stem:
A 16-year-old girl has had cramping pelvic pain with every period since she was 13, and it has worsened each year. She now misses school for two or three days each month, and ibuprofen and paracetamol only partly help. She is not sexually active, and her abdominal examination is normal.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Pelvic inflammatory disease from untreated infection
options.D: Recurrent urinary tract infection of the bladder
options.E: Irritable bowel syndrome with cyclical symptoms

correct_answer: B. Endometriosis causing cyclical period-related pain
why_correct: NICE advises suspecting endometriosis in young women, including those aged 17 and under, with period-related pain that affects daily activities. Progressive pain, missed school and a partial response to simple analgesia fit this, and referral to paediatric and adolescent gynaecology is advised for assessment. Source: NICE NG73, Endometriosis: diagnosis and management, 2017 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease needs sexual exposure and typically causes discharge, fever or intermenstrual pain. C. Appendicitis causes acute migratory pain with fever, not recurring pain tied to every period for years. D. A urinary infection would cause urinary symptoms rather than pain that follows her menstrual cycle. E. Irritable bowel syndrome causes bowel-related pain with altered habit, not pain tied to menstruation.
pearl: Suspect endometriosis in adolescents whose period pain is severe, progressive and disrupts school or daily life, to avoid long diagnostic delay.
thinking: Period pain since menarche, worsening  ↓  Missing school with poor response to analgesia  ↓  Persistent and impairing  ↓  Consider endometriosis
exam_trap: Dismissing adolescent period pain as normal delays diagnosis; routine examination is often normal in endometriosis.
takeaway: Severe, progressive period pain affecting daily life in a teenager should prompt consideration of endometriosis.
notes: AKT stem listed obviously wrong distractors; re-angled to progressive pain with partial analgesic response. Live PAQ922 (15-year-old, primary dysmenorrhoea, key NSAID) is the contrasting picture (static pain, regular flow); learning point differs (diagnosis of endometriosis vs first-line treatment). Reviewer to note borderline similarity of setting.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles, no current hormonal contraception and a negative pregnancy test wants to start a combined oral contraceptive pill today, which is day 12 of her cycle. She asks whether she will be protected straight away.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: She is protected immediately, because the pill works from the first tablet
options.B: She needs no extra protection if she takes the pill at the same time each day
options.C: She should use condoms or avoid sex for the first full week of taking the pill
options.D: She must wait until her next period to start because starting mid-cycle is unsafe
options.E: She should take two tablets daily in the first week to gain rapid protection

correct_answer: C. She should use condoms or avoid sex for the first full week of taking the pill
why_correct: The cycle day on which the pill is started determines whether protection is immediate. Starting in the first few days of the cycle gives immediate cover, but starting at any other time, provided pregnancy is reasonably excluded, needs additional contraception for the first week. Source: NICE CKS, Contraception - combined hormonal methods, Last revised in August 2024.
why_wrong: A. Immediate protection applies only when the pill is started in the first days of the cycle, which is not the case here. B. Regular timing helps efficacy but does not give cover before ovulation is suppressed. D. The pill can be started at any point in the cycle if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. E. Doubling the dose is unsafe, adds side effects and does not speed up protection.
pearl: Starting the combined pill early in the cycle gives immediate cover; starting later needs extra contraception such as condoms for the first week.
thinking: Start combined pill mid-cycle  ↓  Pregnancy reasonably excluded  ↓  Outside early cycle days, ovulation not yet suppressed  ↓  Extra contraception for the first week
exam_trap: A, immediate protection, is the common assumption, but it holds only for starts in the first days of the cycle.
takeaway: A mid-cycle start of the combined pill needs additional contraception for the first week.
notes: AKT item keyed cycle day in a factor-recall format; re-angled to the advice decision. The first-few-days window and 7-day figure are expressed in words (first week) rather than keyed numerically. CKS COC page also lists the Qlaira/Zoely exceptions (9 days), omitted for simplicity; stem uses a standard pill. Live ID037/BX282/PAN6001 cover missed pills, not starting.

stem:
A 24-year-old non-smoker with a normal BMI is about to start a combined oral contraceptive pill. During counselling the nurse explains that the oestrogen component is linked to one uncommon but serious adverse effect that she should be told about.

Which adverse effect is this?

options.A: Blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or the lungs
options.B: Permanent reduction in fertility after stopping the pill
options.C: A higher lifetime chance of developing ovarian cancer
options.D: Loss of bone density leading to early osteoporosis
options.E: Progressive scarring of the liver with long-term use

correct_answer: A. Blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or the lungs
why_correct: Oestrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), even in healthy young women. The absolute risk is small, but it is the key serious adverse effect to explain, and she should be told to seek urgent help for unilateral calf swelling or sudden breathlessness. Source: NHS, Combined pill (patient information); BNF treatment summary, Contraceptives, hormonal.
why_wrong: B. Fertility returns promptly after stopping the pill; it does not cause permanent subfertility. C. Combined pill use is associated with a lower, not higher, risk of ovarian cancer. D. Loss of bone density is a concern with depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, not the combined pill. E. The combined pill does not cause progressive liver scarring.
pearl: Oestrogen in combined hormonal contraception raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, which is why personal and family history of clots is checked before prescribing.
thinking: Combined pill contains oestrogen  ↓  Oestrogen promotes clotting  ↓  Serious adverse effect is venous thromboembolism  ↓  Counsel on calf swelling and sudden breathlessness
exam_trap: Choosing ovarian cancer: the combined pill reduces ovarian cancer risk, so the direction of the association is the trap.
takeaway: The combined pill increases venous thromboembolism risk, so ask about clots in the personal and family history before prescribing.
notes: Re-angled from a bare adverse-effect recall item into a counselling vignette (healthy 24-year-old). Learning point unchanged; no figures. The NHS combined-pill page opened only lists past blood clots in its suitability text, and the BNF treatment summary only mentions CHC with thromboprophylaxis; the VTE link itself is standard teaching (the CKS combined hormonal methods page rendered without readable content, so it is not cited). Reviewer: confirm citation wording acceptable. No live duplicate found (live items cover CHC contraindications, migraine with aura and pill vomiting, not general VTE counselling).
